item.title: African Union envoy calls for shared value chains
item.dc:creator: Sponsor
item.description: China’s policy of allowing goods from 53 African countries to be imported tariff-free will not only help expand African exports but also advance the continent’s industrialisation and build shared value chains with China, the African Union’s top envoy in Beijing says. “We don’t just want to be exporting fruits and vegetables to China, much as […]
item.content:encoded:
China’s policy of allowing goods from 53 African countries to be imported tariff-free will not only help expand African exports but also advance the continent’s industrialisation and build shared value chains with China, the African Union’s top envoy in Beijing says.

“We don’t just want to be exporting fruits and vegetables to China, much as that is extremely important,” said Alhaji Mohamed Sarjoh Bah, the AU’s permanent representative to China. “We also want to use this as an opportunity for us to industrialise.”

His appeal comes as China and African countries celebrate the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations and observe the China-Africa Year of People-to-People Exchanges.

The partnership, rooted in decades of solidarity and mutual respect, has developed into a dynamic relationship marked by expanding practical collaboration, Bah said.

Since May 1 China has provided zero-tariff access to products from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, becoming the first major economy to do so.

Bah described China as “one of the most lucrative markets in the world today”, saying its consumer market of more than 1.4 billion people and with a sizable middle-income group, more than 400 million according to official figures, offers significant opportunities for African exporters.

China imported goods worth 193.8 billion yuan ($28.85 billion) from Africa in May and June, 23.5 per cent more than in the corresponding period last year, China’s Foreign Ministry said. African dried chilli peppers, coffee beans, cashews and wild aquatic products have also secured region-wide market access in China.

The policy could also create opportunities for greater Chinese investment in Africa’s energy, technology, connectivity, infrastructure and agriculture and help African countries process more of their resources locally, Bah said.

Citing lithium as an example, he described a value chain in which some processing takes place in Africa and the rest in China, with the resulting products serving the wider global market. Such an arrangement, he said, would be “mutually reinforcing”.

The media could help Chinese audiences better understand Africa as an investment destination and become more familiar with African products, Bah said.

Caption: Workers sort oranges from Egypt and grapefruits from South Africa at a designated fruit import port in Tongling, Anhui province. CHEN LEI / FOR CHINA DAILY

item.title: Building a more equitable global order
item.dc:creator: Sponsor
item.description: By TESHOME TOGA CHANAKA Te international governance system is facing one of its most serious crises. Growing geopolitical rivalry, weakened multilateral institutions, selective application of international law, and the inability to respond effectively to global challenges — from climate change and pandemics to debt, artificial intelligence and armed conflicts — have exposed the limitations of […]
item.content:encoded:
By TESHOME TOGA CHANAKA

Te international governance system is facing one of its most serious crises. Growing geopolitical rivalry, weakened multilateral institutions, selective application of international law, and the inability to respond effectively to global challenges — from climate change and pandemics to debt, artificial intelligence and armed conflicts — have exposed the limitations of the current global order. Increasingly, countries are calling for a governance system that is more representative, equitable and responsive to the realities of the 21st century.

Against this backdrop, China launched the Global Governance Initiative in 2025, elaborating on it further in 2026. Far from being an isolated endeavour, the GGI builds on a decade of China-led global initiatives, including the Belt and Road Initiative, the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative and the Global Civilisation Initiative.

Together, these initiatives reflect China’s growing effort to shape international co-operation and contribute to the evolving architecture of global governance.

While these initiatives are global in scope, they have attracted particular interest across the Global South. Many developing countries, especially in Africa, Asia and Latin America, have long argued that the current international system does not adequately reflect today’s geopolitical and economic realities. Decision-making in key international institutions remains concentrated among a few powerful states, while developing countries continue to seek greater representation and influence.

The central question, therefore, is whether China’s GGI can help establish a more representative, effective, and inclusive international order amid increasing global fragmentation.

The GGI is best understood as China’s policy response to what Beijing identifies as growing deficits in peace, development, representation, and institutional effectiveness. It does not propose replacing the existing international system or creating parallel institutions. Rather, it calls for reforming and strengthening the United Nations-centred multilateral system to better address contemporary global challenges.

One of the GGI’s principal objectives is to increase the participation of developing countries in global governance. From an African perspective, initiatives that seek to amplify the voice of the Global South deserve careful consideration. Africa represents nearly one-fifth of the world’s population, yet its influence within many international institutions remains limited. A more balanced system of global governance would not only improve legitimacy but also produce decisions that better reflect the interests of the wider international community.

Beyond economic governance, the GGI places considerable emphasis on co-operation in addressing global public goods.

Climate change, public health, digital governance, and artificial intelligence cannot be managed by individual countries acting alone. These challenges require stronger international co-operation, effective multilateral institutions, and greater trust among nations.

Another important pillar of the initiative is the peaceful settlement of disputes.

In an increasingly polarised international environment, the GGI advocates dialogue, consultation and diplomacy over confrontation and unilateral action.

Ultimately, the success of the GGI will lie in its implementation. Like any major international initiative, it must demonstrate transparency, inclusiveness, and tangible results. It must also build confidence across different regions and political systems in order to gain broad international acceptance.

As international discussions on global governance continue, it is essential that Africa and other regions of the Global South actively participate in shaping the outcome. A governance system that genuinely reflects the diversity of today’s world will be stronger, more legitimate, and better equipped to address the challenges that no nation can solve alone.

The future of global governance will ultimately depend not on who leads or initiates the conversation, but on whether the international community can collectively build institutions that are more representative, more accountable, and more responsive to the aspirations of all humanity.

The author is a former ambassador of Ethiopia to China. This is an abridged version of an article that appeared in China Daily. The views don’t necessarily reflect those of China Daily.

Caption: Attendees observe minimally invasive surgical instruments at the launch ceremony of The China-Africa Partnership Programme for Minimally Invasive Medicine in Addis Ababa on July 27. GENG XINNING / XINHUA

item.title: President’s observations on bloc praised as visionary
item.dc:creator: Sponsor
item.description: By LIU JIANQIAO and XU WEIWEI President Xi Jinping’s speeches during the 18th BRICS Summit reflect the wider global community’s aspirations for fairness, stability and shared progress, and present a timely and forward-looking vision for strengthening co-operation among BRICS countries and the wider Global South, international experts say. Maarij Farooq, deputy editor-in-chief of Daily Ittehad […]
item.content:encoded:
By LIU JIANQIAO and XU WEIWEI

President Xi Jinping’s speeches during the 18th BRICS Summit reflect the wider global community’s aspirations for fairness, stability and shared progress, and present a timely and forward-looking vision for strengthening co-operation among BRICS countries and the wider Global South, international experts say.

Maarij Farooq, deputy editor-in-chief of Daily Ittehad Media Group and the Pakistan Economic Network, said Xi’s remarks at the summit “present a timely and forward-looking vision for strengthening co-operation among BRICS countries and the wider Global South”.

Xi’s emphasis on sovereign equality, multilateralism, international law and the peaceful settlement of disputes reflects the growing demand for a more balanced and representative international system, Farooq said.

Xi, when attending the first day of the BRICS Summit on September 12, noted that as it marks the 20th anniversary of its establishment, the BRICS countries have actively explored development paths suited to their own national conditions, setting an example of self-strengthening through unity.

Xi said that the BRICS countries should deepen mutual understanding through communication and dialogue, properly handle differences, and ensure that BRICS co-operation continues to move forward steadily.

Balew Demissie, a senior consultant at the Policy Studies Institute of Ethiopia, said, “President Xi’s call for BRICS to be a pioneer of our times speaks to the wider global community’s aspirations for fairness, stability and shared progress.”

Khalid Taimur Akram, executive director of the Pakistan Research Centre for a Community with Shared Future in Islamabad, said that in his speech, Xi presented a clear vision for the future of BRICS, emphasising the importance of unity, co-operation and shared development among Global South countries.

Experts also hailed China’s dedication to building a fairer and more equitable technology system, which will bring more benefits to the BRICS countries and the broader Global South community.

Xi’s speech offers a compelling and coherent vision of BRICS as a pioneering force that stands firmly on the right side of history, advancing innovation, peace, mutual civilisational learning, and a fairer global governance system, said Dicky Budiman, a senior researcher at both YARSI University in Indonesia and Griffith University in Australia.

Victor Raballa and Yang Gao contributed to this story.

item.title: Xi unveils five initiatives for stronger BRICS
item.dc:creator: Sponsor
item.description: Deeper co-operation essential for greater progress of Global South, Chinese leader says. Zhao Jia and Mo Jingxi report Chinese President Xi Jinping unveiled five initiatives — covering the areas of artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, smart manufacturing, and talent development — to deepen practical co-operation among BRICS countries and bolster the collective […]
item.content:encoded:
Deeper co-operation essential for greater progress of Global South, Chinese leader says. Zhao Jia and Mo Jingxi report

Chinese President Xi Jinping unveiled five initiatives — covering the areas of artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, smart manufacturing, and talent development — to deepen practical co-operation among BRICS countries and bolster the collective strength of the Global South.

Addressing the second session of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi as he wrapped up his two-day participation in the gathering on September 13, Xi stressed that a stronger foundation for co-operation was essential for the expanded grouping to achieve greater progress.

He urged BRICS countries to leverage their close ties with emerging markets and Global South countries, pursuing open co-operation for mutual benefit while safeguarding stable and smooth industrial and supply chains.

They should foster a larger integrated market, build incubators for innovation, upgrade traditional industries, develop emerging industries and deploy future industries, Xi added.

China will be a pioneer in establishing a BRICS AI open source community, and it will support co-operation in developing and applying large language models, hold specialised AI seminars and training courses, and build an open AI ecosystem, Xi said.

He proposed a BRICS special economic zone partnership under which countries could set up an intelligent portal, co-ordinate policies and build a new frontier for open development. China will also host the BRICS Forum on Trade in Services next year to cultivate new drivers of economic and trade co-operation.

Furthermore, China will push for the establishment of a BRICS digital ecosystem cloud platform and conduct digital skills training, technological exchanges and industrial alignment to jointly advance the digital economy, Xi said.

He expressed the country’s readiness to assist fellow BRICS countries in building smart factories and developing standards and norms, jointly promoting manufacturing transformation and upgrading.

Xi also proposed a BRICS engineer cultivation alliance for the joint development of engineers and mutual recognition of competency standards. China will launch a BRICS youth exchange programme for scientific and technological innovation to cultivate more high-calibre talent.

Noting that this year marks the launch of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), Xi said China will continue to pursue high-quality development, expand high-standard opening-up, implement the Global Development Initiative and advance high-quality Belt and Road co-operation to share opportunities and prosper together with other countries.

Liu Ying, a researcher at the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University of China, said that as BRICS marks the 20th anniversary of its founding and moves towards its next “golden decade”, China’s five initiatives respond to the shared development needs of BRICS and the wider Global South.

As the Global South, with its collective rise, has become a key driver of world multipolarity, Xi said that to bring stability to the world and make it a better place, BRICS countries must seize the historical initiative, rally the Global South, be an active, stabilising and positive force in international affairs, and advance the well-being of all humanity.

Caption: Chinese President Xi Jinping with other leaders and officials at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 13. WANG YE / XINHUA

item.title: Ethiopia’s National Emergency Medical Team Earns Landmark WHO Classification
item.dc:creator: Abraham Tekle
item.description: Ethiopia’s National Emergency Medical Team (EMT) has officially received international classification from the World Health Organization (WHO), becoming the first civilian EMT in the WHO African Region to achieve this milestone. Announced by the WHO on September 15, 2026, the verification confirms that the team meets rigorous global standards across governance, clinical services, logistics, information […]
item.content:encoded:
Ethiopia’s National Emergency Medical Team (EMT) has officially received international classification from the World Health Organization (WHO), becoming the first civilian EMT in the WHO African Region to achieve this milestone.

Announced by the WHO on September 15, 2026, the verification confirms that the team meets rigorous global standards across governance, clinical services, logistics, information management, infection control, and sanitation. The classification recognizes the team’s operational readiness to deploy during health emergencies, disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and humanitarian crises worldwide.

The development of the national team was led by the Ministry of Health and the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), supported by technical assistance from the WHO and partners within the Emergency Medical Team Network. As part of the rigorous verification process, the team completed comprehensive assessments and simulation exercises, demonstrating its capability to set up and operate fully functional field hospitals.

“Today is the day our people ask: ‘Are you there for us? Are you prepared for us?’” said Minister of Health Dr. Mekdes Daba. “The successful WHO verification of Ethiopia’s National Emergency Medical Team demonstrates our readiness to protect communities when emergencies strike.”

The national EMT has already proven its capacity domestically, leading response efforts during the Gamo Zone landslide and directing preparedness initiatives for various public health outbreaks. Looking ahead, international partners and emergency responders plan to build on this milestone to further strengthen regional medical emergency response frameworks.

item.title: PM Abiy Tells BRICS Summit Ethiopia Will Pursue Sea Access Solely Through Negotiations
item.dc:creator: Abraham Tekle
item.description: Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed reiterated at the BRICS Summit that Ethiopia will continue seeking access to the sea through diplomatic channels, framing the ambition strictly as an economic priority rather than a security objective. Addressing delegates, Abiy emphasized that maritime access is essential for the landlocked nation of over 120 million people to expand trade, […]
item.content:encoded:
Ethiopian PM Abiy Ahmed reiterated at the BRICS Summit that Ethiopia will continue seeking access to the sea through diplomatic channels, framing the ambition strictly as an economic priority rather than a security objective.

Addressing delegates, Abiy emphasized that maritime access is essential for the landlocked nation of over 120 million people to expand trade, strengthen supply chains, and reduce transport costs.

“For Ethiopia, access to the sea is, first and foremost, an economic imperative,” Abiy said. “Ethiopia will continue to pursue this objective through peaceful and negotiated arrangements.”

Ethiopia’s renewed drive for Red Sea access has heightened regional diplomatic friction. Officials in neighboring countries, including Eritrea, have rejected Addis Ababa’s stance, characterizing sovereign access initiatives as a threat to territorial integrity.

Abiy rejected claims of aggression, stating that securing reliable port access through bilateral agreements would build economic resilience while fostering broader Horn of Africa integration.

item.title: Putin Hails Ethiopia’s ‘Constructive Role’ in BRICS, Invites PM Abiy to Moscow
item.dc:creator: Ashenafi Endale
item.description: Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Ethiopia’s “constructive contribution” to the BRICS alliance and formally invited PM Abiy Ahmed to attend the upcoming Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow (end of October 2026), following bilateral discussions held on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. The encounter began with a moment of high-level personal diplomacy as […]
item.content:encoded:
Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Ethiopia’s “constructive contribution” to the BRICS alliance and formally invited PM Abiy Ahmed to attend the upcoming Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow (end of October 2026), following bilateral discussions held on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi.

The encounter began with a moment of high-level personal diplomacy as the two leaders shared a ride in President Putin’s presidential limousine to review key bilateral priorities ahead of their formal agenda. Details of the discussion were subsequently disclosed during a broader session held in the presence of the two leaders and key officials from Ethiopia side, including EyobTekalign (PhD) – Governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia;GedionTimotheos (PhD) – Minister of Foreign Affairs; and Ambassador Redwan Hussein – Director General of the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS).

During the session, President Putin highlighted that BRICS has grown into a fully-fledged strategic partnership aimed at shaping a fair multipolar world order, praising Ethiopia’s active participation since becoming a full member on January 1, 2024. Remarking on their preliminary talks during the car ride, Putin emphasized that Ethiopia remains a long-standing and reliable partner of Russia on the African continent. Looking ahead, the Russian leader stated that he looks forward to PMAbiy’s participation in the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, where both leaders are scheduled to hold another bilateral session to advance multi-sector agreements.

item.title: UNECA, DHL Express Partner to Boost African SMEs in Cross-Border Trade Under AfCFTA
item.dc:creator: Ashenafi Endale
item.description: The United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) and DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa have signed a landmark three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at helping small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across the continent navigate and scale within intra-African trade. Delivered through DHL’s GoTrade programme, the collaboration provides practical support to help local businesses leverage opportunities […]
item.content:encoded:
The United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) and DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa have signed a landmark three-year Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at helping small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) across the continent navigate and scale within intra-African trade. Delivered through DHL’s GoTrade programme, the collaboration provides practical support to help local businesses leverage opportunities under Regional Economic Communities (RECs) and the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), a single market encompassing over 1.5 billion people.

The strategic partnership establishes a robust framework for cooperation focused on capacity building for women- and youth-owned businesses, digital transformation, joint research, and knowledge sharing on cross-border commerce. As their flagship first engagement, ECA and DHL are launching a joint virtual training series designed to guide African entrepreneurs through practical trade hurdles. This educational initiative will cover essential operational topics including customs procedures, logistics management, e-commerce integration, digital trade tools, regulatory compliance, market access strategies, and trade finance solutions.

While regional integration offers unprecedented access across the continent, small enterprises frequently encounter steep operational barriers. Addressing these challenges, Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa, noted that while many African businesses have strong ambitions to expand beyond local borders, they often face practical obstacles in understanding customs requirements, securing reliable logistics, and navigating unfamiliar regulatory systems. He emphasized that regional integration initiatives like the AfCFTA create immense opportunities, but those opportunities only translate into actual growth when business owners possess the knowledge, confidence, and practical capabilities to act on them.

The initiative builds on DHL’s global GoTrade programme, which has supported over 24,000 SMEs across 50 countries since 2021, including more than 8,000 in Sub-Saharan Africa alone. By targeting private-sector capability, the agreement aligns with ECA projections showing that full implementation of the AfCFTA could boost intra-African trade by 45% by 2045. Through this initial three-year non-exclusive agreement, both organizations aim to establish a repeatable model for unlocking regional market access, driving inclusive economic participation, and strengthening regional value chains across the continent.

item.title: Jigjiga Uncovers Riyadh’s Thread: Unraveling Saudi Arabia’s Expansion into Horn Security
item.dc:creator: Contributor
item.description: The detention of hundreds of Somali soldiers in Ethiopia’s Jigjiga has led to a thread more serious than a simple illegal border crossing: there is a broad, Saudi-funded military program training thousands of recruits in Somalia, with some graduates being prepared to fight alongside the Sudanese army. The detainees, whose numbers are estimated at between […]
item.content:encoded:
The detention of hundreds of Somali soldiers in Ethiopia’s Jigjiga has led to a thread more serious than a simple illegal border crossing: there is a broad, Saudi-funded military program training thousands of recruits in Somalia, with some graduates being prepared to fight alongside the Sudanese army.

The detainees, whose numbers are estimated at between 180 and 900 soldiers, belong to a batch of roughly three thousand recruits who spent more than a year at the Hanano camp in Galmudug state, Somalia. This training program is funded by Saudi Arabia. Jigjiga has thus, for the first time, brought the shadow behind the training program into the spotlight, raising a direct question about what Riyadh is actually funding and the fate of this force after its training ends.

The sensitivity of the issue grows with revelations from various media outlets like Voice of Horn, which specializes in tracking the Horn of Africa. The reports uncovered the Saudi program is broader than the detained batch and includes more than five thousand Somali recruits, trained by military contractors from Romania, Ukraine, South Africa, and Colombia. More seriously, the source speaks of recruits being prepared for later deployment in Sudan to fight alongside the armed forces.

Mogadishu offered an explanation for the soldiers’ crossing. Addressing the detention of the troops in Ethiopia’s Somali Regional State, Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, publicly acknowledged the crossing. Yusuf explained that the soldiers were granted official leave to visit their families after completing over a year of rigorous instruction at Hananbure. He noted that Mogadishu was fully aware of their movements and that the soldiers chose routes cutting through Ethiopian territory to bypass areas controlled by al-Shabaab militants. However, this account explains the reason for the crossing without addressing the nature and scale of the Saudi program or the destination of its graduates. Neither Addis Ababa nor the Somali embassy has issued an independent clarification regarding the incident.

Other media outlets like BML Daily published about direct Saudi funding for training programs and the possibility that some trainees will later be deployed to Sudan’s front lines. The Jigjiga incident does not prove that the detainees themselves were heading to Sudan, but it raises the heavier question: where did the earlier batches go?

The recruitment file extends into Ethiopia as well, with Addis Standard quoting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed as saying that networks are targeting young people from Tigray, including minors, and smuggling them to participate in Sudan’s war, exploiting their humanitarian and economic conditions. There is no evidence linking these networks to the Saudi program, but they reveal the widening recruitment of fighters from the Horn of Africa into the war.

The Sudan Times also assessed that the continued fighting has allowed networks loyal to the Muslim Brotherhood, including the ‘Al-Bara’ ibn Malik Battalion,’ to strengthen their presence within Sudan’s military establishment, linking recruitment from abroad to efforts to reinforce the armed forces with new elements claims on which the parties concerned have not commented.

In this sense, Jigjiga did not merely uncover soldiers who lost their way home; it opened up a larger Saudi file concerning thousands of recruits receiving Riyadh-funded training in Somalia, whose fate after graduation remains unclear meaning the incident will follow a military trajectory that begins with Saudi money in Horn of Africa training camps and ends with fighters on Sudan’s war fronts.

Natnael Gecho is researcher and investigative journalist.

Contributed by Natnael Gecho

item.title: African Leaders Urge Shift to Climate Agency as CCDA-14 Concludes in Addis Ababa
item.dc:creator: Staff Reporter
item.description: Delegates highlighted a severe funding discrepancy, noting that while Africa accounts for less than four percent of global emissions, the continent requires approximately USD277 billion annually through 2030 to fulfill its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Current international financial flows cover only about 11 percent of that requirement. This was disclosed during the fourteenth Conference on […]
item.content:encoded:
Delegates highlighted a severe funding discrepancy, noting that while Africa accounts for less than four percent of global emissions, the continent requires approximately USD277 billion annually through 2030 to fulfill its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Current international financial flows cover only about 11 percent of that requirement.

This was disclosed during the fourteenth Conference on Climate Change and Development in Africa (CCDA-14) concluded last week with a united call for the continent to transition from climate participation to full climate agency. Hosted under the Climate for Development in Africa (ClimDev-Africa) Programme—a joint effort by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (ECA), the African Union Commission (AUC), the African Development Bank (AfDB), and Afreximbank, alongside the Pan African Climate Justice Alliance (PACJA)—the three-day summit established key strategic priorities leading toward COP31 in Antalya and an African-hosted COP32 in Addis Ababa in 2027.

The conference adopted key outcomes prioritizing global governance and climate agency, urging national parliaments to translate global climate pledges directly into binding legislation, budgets, and accountable oversight. On transformative finance and carbon markets, delegates called on developed nations to honor Paris Agreement commitments while encouraging Africa to build high-integrity carbon pricing mechanisms that fund local clean technology and job creation directly. To build resilience, the assembly prioritized integrated early warning systems, calling for expanded support for National Meteorological and Hydrological Services under the Addis Ababa Call to Action.

In response, closing speaker Hanan Morsy, ECA Deputy Executive Secretary, alongside other continental leaders, stressed that Africa’s climate narrative must move beyond vulnerability to focus on actionable, African-led solutions and predictable, non-debt-creating finance.

Addressing economic transformation, the roadmap highlights a just transition for critical minerals, urging mineral-producing African nations to capture local value and processing under the Africa Mining Vision and the AfCFTA. The framework also links circular economy strategies and urban leadership to support cities facing climate-induced displacement, while asserting that agrifood systems and climate-conflict risks must remain central to national adaptation planning. To ensure implementation, CCDA-14 established six technical working committees to track progress and deliver a comprehensive climate finance report at CCDA-XV ahead of COP32 in Ethiopia.
